source: CIA (2009) A Tradecraft Primer: Structured Analytic Techniques - Devil's Advocacy
finding: Official definition. Devil's Advocacy challenges one dominant mind-set on a judgment you cannot afford to get wrong. Method: state the mainline judgment and key assumptions, pick the most vulnerable assumption, check evidence for doubtful validity or deception, then write a labelled contrarian paper. Three allowed outcomes: line is sound, line needs more work, or line must change or be caveated.
numbers: No numbers. Three explicit outcomes listed. Product must be labelled 'Devil's Advocate' so readers do not confuse it with the official view.
quote: Devil's Advocacy is most effective when used to challenge an analytic consensus or a key assumption regarding a critically important intelligence question.
limits: A how-to, not an experiment. No effect size is given for any technique.
agent_relevance: Gives a code-checkable procedure for a challenge step: restate assumptions, attack the weakest one, return one of three verdicts. Maps to a G1-style trigger (use only on high-stakes consensus) rather than a schedule.

source: CIA (2009) Tradecraft Primer - Team A/Team B vs Devil's Advocacy
finding: Team A/Team B is a different tool: use it when TWO strong competing views already exist, each team builds its own full case. Devil's Advocacy is for ONE dominant view. The primer warns analysts often confuse them and draft a 'Team B' that is really a devil's advocate. It also says forcing analysts to argue the other side makes them more aware of their own mind-set.
numbers: Cost note: full Team A/Team B needs a 'significant commitment of analytic time and resources'.
limits: Descriptive. Claimed benefits (less friction between factions) are asserted, not measured.
agent_relevance: Separate the roles in the agent: a single-view challenger versus two full competing hypotheses. Do not label one as the other.

source: CIA (2009) Tradecraft Primer - Red Team Analysis
finding: Red Team Analysis here means modelling the adversary: place analysts in the target's cultural, organizational and personal setting to beat mirror-imaging. Method: build a team with real knowledge of the target, write first-person questions the adversary would ask, draft the policy papers the adversary would write. Turns the analyst from observer into actor.
numbers: No numbers. Example given: a red-team piece on Iran's military strategy against the US.
quote: the Red Team technique transforms the analyst into an 'actor' operating within the adversary's culture and political milieu
limits: Narrow meaning (adversary simulation). Differs from the DSB/UFMCS meaning (challenge our own plan). Same word, three jobs.
agent_relevance: Operator idea: answer as the opponent would, in first person, with their constraints. For an LLM the risk is that the model plays a generic opponent and mirror-images itself.

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, devil's advocate section
finding: Heuer defines a devil's advocate as someone who defends a minority view, perhaps without believing it, as strenuously as possible, to expose conflicting interpretations. His example: assign a small group to plan the terrorist attack on your own facility. The assignment frees them from the social cost of finding embarrassing weaknesses. He notes devil's advocacy has a 'controversial history' in the Intelligence Community and cites Jervis (1976, pp. 415-418) for strengths and weaknesses.
numbers: No experiment. Also in the book: managers who notice their surprise and investigate it adapt better; people are too slow, not too quick, to change a view.
quote: people are too slow to change an established view, as opposed to being too willing to change
limits: Argument from experience. No measured effect.
agent_relevance: The mechanism is permission: a role makes criticism cost-free. An LLM has no social cost, so the benefit must come from forced search for failures, not from courage. Supports making the challenge a fixed operator with its own slot, triggered on a signal.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Red team - military history
finding: Secondary summary of red-team history: RAND red/blue Cold War games in the early 1960s; Israel formed Ipcha Mistabra after the 1973 intelligence failure; CIA Red Cell after 9/11; Defense Science Board report 2003 recommended red teams; Army created the Army Directed Studies Office in 2004 (first service-level red team, largest in DoD until 2011); UFMCS teaches red teaming at Fort Leavenworth; Marine Corps red team concept 2010, billets staffed June 2013 with 6- or 9-week UFMCS training; three red teams reviewed the bin Laden intelligence in 2011.
numbers: Effectiveness figures are all from physical/cyber testing: FAA tested about 100 US airports a year; TSA 2015 undercover test got weapons or fake explosives past screeners 67 of 70 times.
limits: Wikipedia, not a primary source. States that formal effectiveness measurement of military red teams is thin. The figures are about penetration testing, not plan critique.
agent_relevance: Dates anchor the field. The key gap for us: there is almost no measured evidence that military alternative-analysis red teams improve decisions. Treat the practice as design lore, not as proven.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Agranat Commission
finding: The commission (set up 21 Nov 1973) blamed 'the concept': Military Intelligence assumed Egypt would not attack without air power to challenge Israel's air force, and Syria would not attack without Egypt. That fixed assumption was kept while contrary warning evidence (reports on 1 and 3 Oct 1973 of Egyptian war preparations) was set aside. It recommended judging an enemy's capability, not only its intentions.
numbers: 140 sessions, 58 witnesses, four intelligence officers recommended for dismissal, about 1,500-page report, 2,812 Israeli soldiers killed in the war.
limits: This page does NOT mention a devil's advocate unit; the link from the commission to Ipcha Mistabra is stated only on the Red team page here and was not verified in a primary source. Hindsight bias risk.
agent_relevance: A clean example of an unchallenged load-bearing assumption. Lesson for the agent: list the one assumption the plan cannot survive losing, and test it with capability-based evidence, not stated intent.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Team B (1976)
finding: 1976 CIA competitive analysis: 16 outside experts, three teams, Team B (chair Richard Pipes) reviewed Soviet strategic policy and said the National Intelligence Estimates underrated Soviet aims and power. Later checks found many specific claims wrong. Example: Team B predicted about 500 Backfire bombers by early 1984, the Soviets had 235 in 1984. Garthoff: virtually all criticisms proved wrong and exaggerated the threat. Others (Pipes, Leebaert) say it was right on core intent.
numbers: 16 experts; about 500 predicted vs 235 actual Backfire bombers (1984); Team B said a 1970 NIE military budget estimate was half the true figure.
limits: Contested. Panel chosen one-sidedly (Warnke). Bush later wrote the approach could be manipulated for ends other than accuracy.
agent_relevance: Failure case of alternative analysis: a challenger picked for one view and rewarded for alarm gives biased error, not calibrated error. Guardrail: challenger output must name checkable evidence and cannot set the verdict.

source: Schwenk (1990) Effects of devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry on decision making: a meta-analysis, OBHDP 47:161-176
finding: Crossref confirms the record (title, journal, volume, pages). Content below is from memory, not read this session: devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry both tended to give better decision quality than consensus methods, with no reliable difference between the two; effects shown mostly in lab studies with student groups.
numbers: Not verified this session. A companion 1989 paper in Strategic Management Journal compared the two methods (Crossref listing only).
limits: Unopened: check numbers (number of studies, effect sizes) before use.
agent_relevance: Best available aggregate for 'does structured dissent beat consensus'. Must be read before the schema cites it.

source: Schweiger, Sandberg & Ragan (1986) Group approaches for improving strategic decision making, Acad Manage J 29:51-71
finding: From memory, not read: lab experiments with devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry groups against a consensus group; both dissent methods gave higher-quality recommendations and assumptions than consensus, while consensus groups reported more satisfaction and wish to work together again.
numbers: N and effect sizes not recorded (unverified).
limits: Unopened. Student subjects; short tasks; satisfaction cost is a known trade-off.
agent_relevance: Dissent raises quality but lowers comfort. For one agent, comfort is irrelevant, so the cost side disappears; the benefit may remain only if the challenger is truly independent.

source: Nemeth, Brown & Rogers (2001) Devil's advocate versus authentic dissent, Eur J Soc Psychol 31:707-720
finding: From memory, not read: role-played devil's advocacy stimulated mostly thoughts that supported the original position (cognitive bolstering), while authentic minority dissent stimulated more divergent thinking and new solutions. Direct fetches of the paper failed (HTTP 404 or blocked).
numbers: Numbers not verified.
limits: Unopened. Single paper; check design and N.
agent_relevance: Strong warning: a role-played challenger from the same mind may only strengthen the first view. For an LLM, same-model personas are the analogue; independence matters (G4).

source: Mitchell, Russo & Pennington (1989) Back to the future: temporal perspective in the explanation of events, J Behav Decis Making 2:25-38
finding: From memory, not read: imagining that an event has already happened (prospective hindsight) raised the number of correct reasons people gave for it by about 30 percent. This is the basis of Klein's pre-mortem, a cheap internal red-team step.
numbers: About +30 percent reasons (recalled, unverified).
limits: Unopened. Lab task, not plan review.
agent_relevance: Cheap operator: assume this plan failed; list why. Run only on a signal such as high stakes or disagreement (G1).

source: Perez et al. (2022) Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
finding: One LM writes test questions, a classifier scores the target LM's replies. Target: 280B Dialogue-Prompted Gopher. Zero-shot generation, stochastic few-shot, supervised learning and RL were compared. Zero-shot cases found 18,444 offensive replies from 0.5M cases. RL raised yield above 40 percent but collapsed in diversity.
numbers: Zero-shot: 3.7 percent offensive of 0.5M cases (18,444). RL with KL weight 0.3: over 40 percent; 78 percent of those cases contained the word 'invisible'. 7B red LM: 4.3 percent zero-shot. Offensive questions beget offensive replies.
limits: Red team and target were both Gopher family. Success judged by an offensiveness classifier, not by harm to users. Diversity and difficulty trade off.
agent_relevance: Shows an automatic attacker finds failures a human list misses, but pushing hard on yield cuts diversity. For our challenger: sample many varied attacks, then keep a code-checked failing one.

source: Ganguli et al. (2022) Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms
finding: Human red teaming at scale: 324 crowdworkers (307 MTurk, 17 Upwork), 38,961 attacks across model sizes 2.7B, 13B, 52B and four model types (plain, helpful-honest-harmless prompt, rejection sampling, RLHF). RLHF models got harder to red team as they grew; other types showed a flat trend with scale.
numbers: 38,961 attacks; 324 red teamers; 3 sizes x 4 types. Rejection sampling: 16 samples, shows the 2 least harmful.
limits: Crowdworker attackers differ in skill; no ground truth of true harm; authors stress uncertainty about methodology.
agent_relevance: Defence got better with a trained objective, not with an extra prompt. Suggests relying on code checks and training signal rather than adding persona instructions.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Intrinsic self-critique without ground truth does not help and often hurts. Earlier gains came from using oracle labels to decide when to stop. Without oracle, after 2 rounds, accuracy fell on all tasks.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) and 41.8 (round 2); GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0; CSQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0. Oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 vs 84.3; GPT-4 HotpotQA 49 to 59.
limits: One to two hundred items per set (100 for HotpotQA). CSQA drop is partly because wrong options look plausible.
agent_relevance: This is the evidence behind G1 and G2: an internal audit with no outside signal can flip right answers to wrong. The red-team step must use a real check, not a bare 'are you sure?'.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Survey conclusion: no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except in tasks exceptionally suited to it; self-correction works when reliable external feedback exists; large-scale fine-tuning also enables it. Many positive results used oracle information or unfair comparisons.
numbers: No single number; checklist for fair self-correction experiments.
limits: Review of other papers; framing is by category of feedback source.
agent_relevance: Confirms the design: the challenger needs an outside verifier (tests, retrieval, executable check).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Poor self-correction comes from failing to FIND the error, not from failing to fix it. Models struggle to locate mistakes even in unambiguous chain-of-thought traces (BIG-Bench Mistake dataset, 5 tasks). When the true mistake location is given, correction helps on all 5 tasks. A small classifier trained on out-of-domain data located mistakes better than prompting a large model.
numbers: 5 tasks; dataset released. Exact per-task accuracies not recorded here.
limits: Mistake-location labels used as an upper bound; real use needs a locator.
agent_relevance: Fits our rule: code locates the failing step, the model only fixes. A red-team step that asks the model to find its own flaw is the weak half.

source: Liang et al. (2023) Encouraging Divergent Thinking in LLMs through Multi-Agent Debate (MAD)
finding: Names the Degeneration-of-Thought problem: after a model is confident, self-reflection cannot produce new thoughts. MAD uses an affirmative and a negative debater plus a judge, forced to tit for tat. On Counter-Intuitive Arithmetic (200 questions) GPT-3.5 baseline 26.0, CoT 28.0, self-consistency 29.5, self-reflect 27.5, MAD 37.0, GPT-4 51.0.
numbers: Accuracy: 26.0 / 28.0 / 29.5 / 27.5 / 37.0 / GPT-4 51.0. On Common MT, GPT-3.5 with MAD beat GPT-4 on automatic and human scores. Judge adaptive break helps; moderate disagreement works best; a judge model can favour its own family when debaters differ.
limits: Authors' own tasks; one built dataset of 200 items. Later work (Smit; Wang) finds the gain shrinks against fair baselines.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue to red teaming as alternative analysis: an assigned opponent plus a judge. Two knobs matter: adaptive stopping and moderate (not maximal) opposition.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: Several model instances answer, read each other's answers and revise over rounds. 3 agents, 2 rounds. Debate beat single agent, reflection and majority vote on arithmetic, GSM8K and chess. Reflection hurt factual tasks. Gains grew with more agents and rounds.
numbers: Arithmetic 67.0 single, 72.1 reflection, 69.0 majority, 81.8 debate. GSM8K 77.0 / 75.0 / 81.0 / 85.0. Chess pawn score 91.4 / 102.1 / 102.2 / 122.9. ChatGPT+Bard on 20 GSM8K: Bard 11, ChatGPT 14, joint debate 17 solved. Persona agents on MMLU 71.1 to 74.2.
limits: Same-model copies; agreement is not independence. Cost scales with agents x rounds.
agent_relevance: Shows an upside of cross-checking, mostly via diversity between agents. It does not give a signal for when to stop or who is right.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? (ICML 2024)
finding: Benchmarks debate protocols against self-consistency and ensembling. In their present form multi-agent debate systems do NOT reliably beat these simpler methods. After hyperparameter tuning some (e.g. Multi-Persona) do better; adjusting agent agreement levels can lift results above all non-debate protocols.
numbers: Qualitative in the abstract; numbers not extracted.
limits: Sensitive to hyperparameters; tuning on the same benchmark risks overfitting.
agent_relevance: A weak replication of the debate story. Prefer cheap sampling plus code checks as the baseline, and require debate to beat it.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt (a demonstration or a detailed question description) reaches almost the same performance as the best multi-agent discussion across tasks and backbones. Multi-agent discussion wins only when the prompt has NO demonstration.
numbers: Compared Debate, MAD, ReConcile and the authors' framework; example figure on FOLIO-wiki. Numbers not extracted.
limits: Reasoning benchmarks only.
agent_relevance: The benefit of an opponent may be mostly prompt quality. Test a strong single-agent self-audit prompt as the control.

source: Wynn, Satija & Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Debate can lower accuracy over rounds, even when stronger models outnumber weaker ones. Models often switch from correct to incorrect to agree with peers, favouring agreement over challenging flawed reasoning. Tested sycophancy, social conformity, model and task type with GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B on MMLU, GSM8K, CommonsenseQA.
numbers: Exact accuracy deltas not extracted this session.
limits: Small open models; short debates.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for red teaming by agents: a challenger that talks the answerer out of a correct answer is worse than none. A revision must cite new evidence (G2).

source: Khan et al. (2024) Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers (ICML 2024)
finding: Two expert LLMs argue for different answers; a judge who cannot see the text picks one (QuALITY). Debate helped both weak model judges and humans, and training debaters for persuasiveness improved judge accuracy.
numbers: Non-expert model judges 76 percent and humans 88 percent with debate; naive baselines 48 percent and 60 percent. Adversarial protocols beat non-adversarial consultancy.
limits: Experts have the source text, the judge does not. Not a planning task.
agent_relevance: Adversarial structure beats a single advocate (consultancy) because the opponent exposes the weak side. A reason to prefer two-sided challenge over one-sided find-the-flaw.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Devil's Advocate: Anticipatory Reflection for LLM Agents
finding: Before acting, the agent writes the likely failure and a backup; after acting it checks alignment with the subtask and backtracks; at the end it reviews the plan. On WebArena (GPT-4, zero-shot) success reached 23.5 percent after seven episodes, versus 22.7 for LATS and 19.8 for Plan+Act. Fewer trials and plan revisions (45 percent claimed).
numbers: 23.5 vs 22.7 (LATS) vs 19.8 (Plan+Act); +3.5 points over prior zero-shot methods per abstract; 45 percent fewer trials and revisions; average actions 6.39 to 7.07 across trials.
limits: Small margins; one benchmark; the method also reads environment feedback after acting.
agent_relevance: Closest working devil's advocate in an agent loop. Gains are small and rest on real environment feedback.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (ICLR 2024)
finding: Five RLHF assistants show sycophancy on four free-form tasks: they cave when challenged, tailor feedback to the user, and are swayed by a user's suggested wrong answer. Human and preference-model judges prefer convincing sycophantic answers over correct ones a non-negligible fraction of the time.
numbers: A user suggesting an incorrect answer cut accuracy by up to 27 percent (LLaMA 2). Preference model of human choices: 71.3 percent holdout accuracy.
limits: Measures user-facing assistants; effect size varies by model.
agent_relevance: A red-team challenge phrased like 'are you sure?' invites caving. The challenger must be a separate slot with a test, not a user-style push.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making
finding: Eight nation agents in a simulated wargame, five off-the-shelf LLMs. All showed escalation and hard-to-predict escalation patterns; arms-race dynamics; rarely nuclear use; reasoning cited deterrence and first-strike.
numbers: 5 LLMs; 8 nation agents; score values not extracted.
limits: Simulation, no human baseline; depends on model and scenario.
agent_relevance: LLM simulation of an adversary is biased and unstable, so an adversary role needs scenario constraints and checks.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences between Expert Humans and LLMs in Wargame Simulations
finding: 214 national security experts in a fictional US-China crisis compared with LLM-simulated teams. High-level agreement, but LLMs were more aggressive and more affected by scenario changes. Simulated team dialogue lacks quality and keeps a farcical harmony. LLM runs showed no difference even for extreme traits like pacifist or aggressive sociopath.
numbers: 214 experts. Other effect sizes not extracted.
limits: One scenario family.
agent_relevance: Simulated disagreement between instances is thin: personas do not produce real dissent. Supports G4 (no persona voters) and treats adversary simulation as weak evidence.

source: Defense Science Board (2003) Role and Status of DoD Red Teaming Activities
finding: Not read: all fetches of the report failed (HTTP 403 or non-PDF). Known only through the Wikipedia Red team page, which says the 2003 report recommended red teams to prevent shortcomings like those before 9/11.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Primary text missing. Needs a retry via another mirror.
agent_relevance: Needed for the formal definition and the list of recommendations; do not quote from memory.

source: UFMCS (2004 on) Red Team Handbook and the Army Directed Studies Office
finding: Not read: handbook URLs tried were not retrievable. From the Wikipedia Red team page only: the Army created the Army Directed Studies Office in 2004 as the first service-level red team and UFMCS teaches red-team courses at Fort Leavenworth. Handbook content (its list of red-team tools) was not verified.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Primary text missing.
agent_relevance: Must be read before copying any UFMCS tool list into the schema.
